_doc: VO is the timing backbone — scene length = measured VO duration + 0.6s pad, NOT target_sec. Target ~2:50 (170s), hard cap 180s. ReceiptGuard heist arc: cold open (a confident hallucination + real-world stakes) → the ask → how it can't lie → LIVE run (baseline hallucinates, guard verifies + ships, on Alibaba FC) → LIVE catch (inject a fabrication, GSAR recovery) → SplitScreen contrast (without vs with) → LIVE ledger reveal (tamper breaks chain) → MCP server (three tools) → benchmark + ablation reframe → logo. capture:null = motion graphic; capture:'captures/x' = LIVE app footage over http://localhost:8000 (never a recreation).

scenes.vo: A support agent just told a customer their refund was approved. Two hundred and forty dollars, credited. It sounds finished. It sounds confident.

Except that refund never happened — the agent made the tool result up. A tribunal has already held an airline liable for exactly this: a support chatbot that invented a refund policy. ReceiptGuard makes that structurally impossible.

graphic_props.line: Tool result hallucinated — no refund record exists.

scenes.vo: So we give it one job. Resolve this refund ticket, end to end — and prove every tool result it acts on.

graphic_props.label: The one job
graphic_props.task: Resolve this refund ticket — and prove every tool result

scenes.vo: Every tool call runs through a gateway that signs its result with an unforgeable receipt. Every claim the agent writes is cross-checked against those receipts. No receipt, no ship.

graphic_props.line: Every tool result is signed. Every claim is cross-checked.

scenes.vo: Watch it live, on Alibaba Function Compute. It plans with Qwen3-Max, runs real tools through a gateway that signs every result, and a cheap Qwen-Flash pass types every claim back to a receipt. On the left, the baseline hallucinates. On the right, ReceiptGuard ships only what's backed.

Now inject a fabrication it never earned — a fifty-dollar goodwill credit with no receipt. The baseline ships the lie. ReceiptGuard flags the unbacked claim, regenerates, and rewrites a clean, grounded reply — and Qwen3-Max's reasoning shows exactly why.

Here's the difference. Without the guard, an agent ships fabrications straight to your customers and your books. With it, every unbacked claim is blocked before it commits — and anything outside policy goes to a human.

leftItems.text: …none of those tools were ever called.

rightItems.text: Out of policy → escalated to a human.

scenes.vo: Every decision lands on an append-only, tamper-evident ledger. Signed receipts, hash-chained with SHA-256. Change one row and the whole chain breaks, visibly — that's EU AI Act record-keeping, built in from the start.

And it's not a closed demo — ReceiptGuard is an installable MCP server. Any client can call the whole safety loop as three tools: run the guarded autopilot, verify claims, list scenarios. Drop it in front of any agent that touches money.

graphic_props.kicker: Not a closed demo — an MCP server

scenes.vo: On our self-authored adversarial set: a hundred percent of fabrications caught, zero false positives. Turn the receipt check off and detection falls to sixty-seven percent. A raw judge with no receipts? A hundred percent false positives.

graphic_props.sub: 0% false positives · ablation 66.7% · self-authored adversarial set

scenes.vo: ReceiptGuard. A support autopilot that acts only on what it can prove, and escalates the rest to humans. Built on Qwen3-Max, Qwen-Flash, and Alibaba Function Compute.

graphic_props.tagline: Acts only on what it can prove.
